title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Monday; 6/7 days of sales vs. 7/7 in baseline. Historical pattern shows ~14% drop on similar closures.

drivers.name: Price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: Past 1.5% price hikes (e.g., 2026-09-28) showed ~1.2% sales drop (noise-adjusted).

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 438.2. The store is closed Monday, reducing the selling days from 7 to 6, implying a 14.3% sales drop. The price increased 1.5%, and past data shows a 1.2% drop in sales at similar price hikes (noise-adjusted). No other drivers (events, promotions) are active. The classical model’s 1.00 multiplier ignores the closure and price, so we adjust. The closure effect is strong and certain; the price effect is modest and supported by past behavior. We combine multiplicatively and shrink slightly due to limited data on price sensitivity.

brief:
PRODUCT: Bananas (per lb) | category Produce | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.1 - 556.5 | 10%-90%: 346.2 - 529.5

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
